clue.text: Making one pound the old-time tanner is furious

parts.note: L, from the Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound sterling
I is the Roman numeral for one
a tanner was slang for the old British sixpence, written VId (six pence, d being the old penny)

explanation.surface: Someone forced to pay a whole pound for an old sixpence is hopping mad.
explanation.walkthrough: A tanner was the pre-decimal British sixpence, written as VI (six) followed by d, the old abbreviation for a penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Livid is everyday English for extremely angry, the same intensity as raging.

clue.text: In which we see all but the first of these letters

definitions.text: In which we see all but the first of these letters

parts.words: In which we see all but the first of these letters
parts.note: the clue is printed with only its opening letter as a capital, so every letter after the first is in small type

explanation.walkthrough: Look at the clue itself: only the I of 'In' is a capital; the rest are small letters, the kind printers kept in the bottom tray.
explanation.definitionFit: Small letters, as opposed to capitals, are called lowercase, from the printer's lower tray of type.

clue.text: Roman goddess as a fire-raiser

definitions.meaning: the Roman goddess of the hearth and household
a brand of short wax match, which raises a flame

explanation.surface: A Roman deity is cast as an arsonist.
explanation.definitionFit: Vesta was the Roman hearth goddess, and her name was given to a kind of match used to strike fire.

clue.text: Ten per cent deducted if we get married after the beginning of last month

indicators.note: after puts the marriage piece behind the month piece
only the opening part of the word for the last month is kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: December is the last month of the year
one of the couple says I mated, meaning I took a partner

explanation.surface: A tenth is docked from something if a couple wed early in December.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's loose cryptic reads the answer as 'Dec, I mated': one partner reporting a December wedding. Decimate first meant killing one soldier in ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Decimated originally meant reduced by a tenth, the Roman punishment of killing one man in every ten.

clue.text: Amazed to see a good man 'unted by dogs

parts.note: ST, short for saint, is the crossword's usual good man
hunted by dogs is hounded; the clue drops the h Cockney-style, so the h is dropped from hounded too

explanation.surface: Someone is startled to see a respectable man being chased by hounds, in a Cockney voice.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ''unted' shows a dropped h, as a Cockney speaker would say it; the same h is dropped from the synonym, hounded.
explanation.definitionFit: To be amazed is to be stunned with surprise, a synonym pair.

clue.text: A scholar with true form as an old cricketing gentleman

parts.note: MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate scholar

indicators.note: form here means a shape the letters are put into, so the word true is rearranged

explanation.surface: A learned man in fine form plays as a gentleman cricketer of old.
explanation.walkthrough: In old English cricket, unpaid 'Gentlemen' played against paid 'Players'; 'form' rearranges TRUE into TEUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Unpaid cricketers of old were called Gentlemen, as opposed to professional Players, so a gentleman was a non-professional.

clue.text: Burlesque flier's start

definitions.meaning: the moment an aircraft leaves the ground

explanation.definitionFit: A take-off is both a comic impersonation and an aeroplane's departure into the air.

clue.text: Claudius to Hamlet's recipient of pledge

definitions.meaning: Claudius is the brother of Hamlet's father in Shakespeare's play
old slang for a pawnbroker, who takes goods as pledges

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Claudius is the one Hamlet makes a promise to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncle' is old British slang for a pawnbroker, who receives goods pledged against a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudius is the brother of Hamlet's father, and a pawnbroker was jokingly called by the same family title.

clue.text: This might go to the wall — as might Fido with it?

definitions.text: This might go to the wall
definitions.meaning: a kind of paint applied to walls
a dog with this disease might go to the wall, that is, die

explanation.surface: Paint goes on walls, and a sick dog might too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to the wall' means to be applied to a wall, and also to fail or perish; Fido is a stock name for a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Distemper is both a water-based wall paint and a serious viral disease of dogs.

clue.text: What one did in a house turned indecent before the end of it

definitions.text: What one did in a house

indicators.note: turned means turned round, so the word for indecent is read backwards

parts.note: lewd means indecent

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, here of it

explanation.surface: Life inside a home turned obscene just before it finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' reverses LEWD to DWEL; 'the end of it' gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: To have dwelt somewhere is to have lived there, which is what one did in a house.

clue.text: Sounds like the youth leader's expert witticism

indicators.note: the clue openly says the next words are to be heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: the leader of youth is its first letter Y; with the 's added this is Y's
crack, as in a crack shot, means expert

explanation.surface: Apparently a youth club organiser made a clever joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Y's, the letter Y with 's, is pronounced exactly like 'wise'; 'expert' gives CRACK, as in a crack shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisecrack is a smart quip, a kind of witticism.

clue.text: A mark of class

parts.note: read as the painted forehead sign in India that shows a person's hereditary social group; the answer is that group itself

explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a fixed hereditary social class in Hindu society, and the forehead mark is named after it.

clue.text: "This blessed plot, this earth, this ——, this England" (Richard II)

definitions.text: "This blessed plot, this earth, this ——, this England" (Richard II)

parts.words: "This blessed plot, this earth, this ——, this England" (Richard II)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from John of Gaunt's famous speech in Shakespeare's Richard II, where the missing word means kingdom

explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Gaunt's line is a synonym for kingdom or domain.

clue.text: Work in one's natural medium producing The Barrett-Browning Match

indicators.note: the clue word in places the piece for work inside the piece for a natural medium

parts.note: to be in one's element is to be in one's natural surroundings
OP, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: Someone working happily where they feel at home produces a famous Victorian love match.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Barrett secretly ran off with the poet Robert Browning in 1846 to marry against her father's wishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrett and Browning's marriage came about by running away together in secret, which is eloping.

clue.text: Judge rear to' be out of order without central portion

annotationWithheld.why: Judge rear to be out of order without central portion (7): the fodder 'rear to be' gives REARTOBE, with no I, and no reading of 'without central portion' turns it into ARBITER; scan confirms the wording
annotationWithheld.clue: Judge rear to' be out of order without central portion

clue.text: Could pons asinorum be so described? It could trigger a bomb

definitions.text: Could pons asinorum be so described?
definitions.meaning: the bridge of asses, Euclid's theorem that catches out slow learners, is a snare for fools
a concealed device set to explode when touched

explanation.surface: A geometry puzzle that trips up dunces is likened to a hidden explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: Pons asinorum, 'bridge of asses', is Euclid's proposition about isosceles triangles, said to defeat dim pupils, so a trap for boobies.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a snare for dunces, and in war a hidden device set off by an unwary victim.

clue.text: Blunder the French funambulist should avoid

definitions.meaning: a social gaffe or embarrassing mistake
French for false step; a tightrope walker must never make a false step

explanation.surface: A tightrope walker from France has one thing never to do.
explanation.definitionFit: A faux pas is a social slip, and literally in French a false step, which a rope-walker must avoid.

clue.text: Turned out tricky without an instructor

indicators.note: tricky suggests the letters of turned out have been arranged deceptively into a new order

explanation.surface: Something proved difficult because there was no teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' rearranges the letters of TURNED OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Untutored means untaught, having had no teacher.

clue.text: Suffering a flesh-wound, retired from contest

definitions.meaning: having the skin grazed by claws or nails
withdrawn from a race or match before the start

explanation.surface: A competitor with a minor injury pulls out of the event.
explanation.definitionFit: Scratched means grazed on the skin, and a horse or player withdrawn from an event is also scratched.

clue.text: Speaker's introductions one axed or revised

indicators.note: something revised has been reworked, so the letters of the fodder are put into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An orator's opening remarks were cut and rewritten by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revised' tells you to rearrange I (one) with AXED and OR; the plural ending -IA is the Latin form.
explanation.definitionFit: An exordium is the opening part of a speech or treatise; the plural is the Latin form.

clue.text: Did its capital rise, from its ashes?

definitions.text: Did its capital rise, from its ashes?

parts.words: Did its capital rise, from its ashes?
parts.note: the US state whose capital is named after the mythical bird reborn from its own ashes

explanation.walkthrough: The state capital is Phoenix, named after the bird of legend that is reborn from the ashes of its own pyre.
explanation.definitionFit: The US state is defined through its capital city, which shares its name with the reborn bird of myth.

clue.text: Terrace put out by a food supplier

indicators.note: put out here means disordered, so the letters of terrace are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who supplies food has set out tables on a terrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like putting out tables, but it is the signal to rearrange TERRACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A caterer is a business that supplies food and drink for events.

clue.text: Happy with opening of course on Spanish wine

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, here of course

parts.note: tent is an old name for a deep red Spanish wine

explanation.surface: Someone is cheerful after starting a meal with Spanish wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Tent is an old word for a dark red Spanish wine, from Spanish tinto.
explanation.definitionFit: To be content is to be satisfied and at ease, close to happy.

clue.text: One advised to try the DIY cure

definitions.text: One advised to try the DIY cure

parts.words: One advised to try the DIY cure
parts.note: refers to the proverb telling a doctor to heal himself, the do-it-yourself remedy

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'Physician, heal thyself' (Luke 4:23) tells the healer to treat himself first, which the clue calls a DIY cure.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb addresses a doctor, telling the healer to cure himself.

clue.text: One in two is a sort of horse

indicators.note: in puts the piece for one inside the abbreviation for two

parts.note: pr is the abbreviation for pair, two of something
an ace is a one in cards and dice

explanation.surface: One horse out of a pair is of a particular breed.
explanation.walkthrough: PR is the standard abbreviation for pair; ACE is the one in a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A pacer is a harness-racing horse that moves both legs on one side together.

clue.text: Sort of sugar that may be dangerous for airmen

definitions.meaning: the fine powdered sugar used for cake coatings

definitions.text: that may be dangerous for airmen
definitions.meaning: ice forming on an aircraft's wings, which can bring it down

explanation.surface: A sweet ingredient is also a hazard for pilots.
explanation.definitionFit: Icing sugar is a fine powdered sugar, and ice building up on wings is a known flying hazard.

clue.text: Tom's backing it, it's understood

indicators.note: backing here means going backwards, so the word for Tom is read in reverse

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: Someone says that Tom supports the idea, as everyone knows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like supporting, but it reverses CAT to give TAC.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tacit is implied without being spoken, so it is silently understood.

clue.text: Cautious of Scylla's opposite number losing bids perhaps

indicators.note: losing tells you letters are dropped from the name of the sea monster

parts.note: in Greek myth the whirlpool monster on the far side of the strait from Scylla
the letters of bids, perhaps in some other order; here as they stand in the monster's name

explanation.surface: Someone is wary of the monster facing Scylla, which might lose its bids.
explanation.walkthrough: Scylla and Charybdis faced each other across the Strait of Messina; 'bids perhaps' gives BDIS, a rearrangement of BIDS, which 'losing' takes from the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Chary means wary or careful, reluctant to take risks.

clue.text: Inhabitant of the Palace has choice of keys, I conclude

indicators.note: the clue says I conclude, so the letter I comes at the end

parts.note: a choice between the musical keys C and G is C or G

explanation.surface: A resident of Buckingham Palace is given the choice of keys, someone deduces.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen's corgis lived at Buckingham Palace. 'Keys' looks like door keys but means musical keys, read as 'C or G'.
explanation.definitionFit: Corgis were the famous pet dogs of the British royal family, living in Buckingham Palace.

clue.text: Stretch too far, so everyone finished first, say?

indicators.note: say at the end tells the solver the phrase is to be heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: everyone is each and finished is over; with over put first this is over each

explanation.surface: A runner pushes too hard, so that everyone crosses the line first.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British accent 'over each' runs together to sound like the answer, the linking R appearing in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To overreach is to reach or strain beyond one's limit.

clue.text: Turn up — said to be raining outside hateful!

indicators.note: outside means the word for reigning goes around the turned-up piece

parts.note: raining spoken sounds like reigning, and reigning is regnant

indicators.note: turn tells you to turn the little word up around so it reads backwards

explanation.surface: Someone shows up, complaining that the rain outside is awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' reverses UP to PU; 'said to be raining' gives 'reigning' by sound, which is REGNANT, and 'outside' wraps it around PU.
explanation.definitionFit: Something repugnant is so offensive it provokes hatred or disgust.

clue.text: Wood-nymph's publicity for prohibition?

parts.note: dry describes a region where alcohol is banned, as under Prohibition
an ad is a piece of advertising, publicity

explanation.surface: A forest spirit is doing publicity in favour of banning drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'publicity for prohibition' reads as an advertisement promoting being dry, a DRY AD.
explanation.definitionFit: A dryad is a tree spirit of Greek myth, a nymph of the woods.
